newsitem.title: USA: Music companies profit growth slows with downturn.
newsitem.headline: Music companies profit growth slows with downturn.

text.p: Flat sales and a poor market are cooling the quarterly profits of big record labels, long considered the mainstay of the entertainment industry.

On Tuesday, Time Warner Inc's Warner Music Group, the nation's leading label with a 22 percent share of the U.S. record market, posted fourth-quarter earnings before interest tax depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) of $290 million, compared with $295 million in 1995.

"Warner Music's results were essentially in line with modest expectations," said Jill Krutick, analyst with Smith Barney. "The industry remains in a fairly difficult state and the slump is not expected to turn around in the near-term."
Hartsdale, N.Y.-based Soundscan reported total U.S. album sales for 1996 edged to 616.6 million from 616.3 million in 1995.

Overcapacity at the retail level, lack of any breakaway hit acts, and the nearing end of a trend to replace vinyl albums with compact discs have slowed sales, which for more than a decade had grown from 12 to 20 percent a year.
For the full year, Warner Music's EBITDA was $744 million, compared with $690 million for 1995, which includes an $85 million one-time charge.
"The fact that Warner was able to show flat numbers was better than the rest of the industry, with the exception of MCA (Universal)," said Chris Dixon, analyst with PaineWebber.

While Warner, with a roster of stars including big seller Alanis Morissette and R.E.M, struggles to maintain its No. 1 position, Universal Music, the music arm of Seagram Co Ltd and formerly called MCA Music, has risen from the bottom to become a market leader.
Analysts and industry sources attribute its rise to its newly acquired 50 percent ownerhip in Interscope Records, which despite anti-rap opponents, has consistently topped music charts.

"Universal's investment in its music group's new labels and artists this past year led to significantly higher revenues and profits in the quarter," said Edgar Bronfman, president and chief executive officer of Seagram in a statement with the company's earnings in late January.

Seagram said most of Universal's 13 percent increase in earnings EBITDA came from music and theme parks. Seagram's music revenues for the second quarter rose to $45 million from $27 million a year ago.

Because records are cheaper to make than movies, labels have long been considered the crown jewels of their parent entertainment counterparts. Higher earnings from Sony Music offest a weak quarter at Sony Pictures, dragged down by some disappointments at the box office.
Sony Music's sales rose 16 percent to $1.6 billion, buoyed by Celine Dion's hit, "Falling Into You."

Polygram NV is singing a different tune, however. Analysts expect Polygram, 75 percent owned by Philips Electronics NV, to report sharply lower profits on Wednesday as it feels the effect of $90 million charge announced last year to reflect a cutback in 400 jobs worldwide to restructure its music operations. Polygram, whose artists include U2 and The Cranberries, has said it expects operating results before charges to be flat or slightly below 1995 levels due to sluggish music sales.
